{{clear}} == 記録 == According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ōwakako no Mikoto learned the classics under the tutelage of 【ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐】 and 【ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁】, who were brought from {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} as tribute. However, the historical veracity of these details is uncertain.『日本書紀』 records that he learned the classics from Adochigi and Ōnin, but their historicity cannot be confirmed. [https://kotobank.jp/word/阿直岐 {{ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐}}] [https://kotobank.jp/word/王仁 {{ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁}}]. Tsuda Sayokichi regarded these as later fabrications.{{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤正二|date=2006-07-01|title=研究 on Japanese Nature: Transformation and Decline|series=斎藤正二著作選集|publisher=八坂書房|page=129}}{{Cite book|和書|author=菅原信海|date=1996-01-01|title=Japanese Thought and Syncretism|publisher=春秋社|page=24}} It is also suggested that Adochigi and Ōnin were of Chinese origin from Baekje.{{Cite book|和書|author=馬渕和夫|date=1999-01-01|title=History of the Japanese Language Studies|publisher=笠間書院|page=17}} According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, he was favored by his father, Emperor Suinin.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 15th and 16th year entries. In the 28th year of Suinin Tennō’s reign, a letter from the 【ill|Goguryeo|ja|高句麗】 pointed out an offense, which he repudiated.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 28th year, September entry. In the 40th year of Suinin Tennō’s reign (Lunisolar January), he was designated Crown Prince.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 40th year, January entry. In the following year, after the emperor's death, Ōwakako no Mikoto did not ascend the throne but instead shared the imperial succession with his half-brother, Emperor Nintoku. Amid this, his half-brother, {{ill|Ōyama no Mikoto|ja|大山守皇子}}, resentful at not being named Crown Prince, attempted to assassinate him. Ōyama no Mikoto's conspiracy was forewarned by Ōwakako no Mikoto, leading to Ōyama no Mikoto’s own demise. At that moment, a poem was composed directed at Ōyama no Mikoto’s remains:Interpretations of the classical reading and transliteration are based on the annotations and translations by Kenji Kojima, et al. in 『日本書紀』. {{Cquote|Chihayabito, across the Uji River, I shall raise the bow of catalpa wood; Though my heart wishes to strike, though it wishes to seize, In truth, I recall you, and in the far reaches, I recall my sister. In sorrow I hold you in my thoughts, yet I do not strike. (catalpa bow)} Afterward, Ōwakako no Mikoto resided at the palace known as {{ill|Ujidō no Miyako|ja|菟道宮}}, and for three years he alternated the throne with Ōyama no Mikoto. Troubled by the prospect that the long interregnum might cause national disarray, he eventually chose to end the sharing by taking his own life. In response, his half-brother was stricken with grief; from Nanba (【ill|Osaka|ja|大阪】) to Ujidō, rituals to summon the spirit were performed, and it is said that Ōwakako no Mikoto was revived, ordered that his half-sister, {{ill|Yata no Hime|ja|八田皇女}}, be received into the palace, and then passed away again.『日本書紀』, before Emperor Nintoku’s accession. === 古事記 === The {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} begins with the account of the consort, Miyanushi Yagahime (宮主矢河枝比売), who resided in Kobata (present-day {{ill|Kobata, Uji|ja|木幡}} in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture) where Emperor Suinin encountered her, leading to the birth of Ōwakako no Mikoto. Following this, the narrative aligns with that of the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. The poem composed at the time of Ōyama no Mikoto’s death is also included with almost identical wording.Annotations and transliterations are based on Kenji Kojima, et al., 『古事記』 (岩波文庫, 1963). However, regarding imperial succession, the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} simply states that Ōwakako no Mikoto died young, leading to Emperor Nintoku’s accession. === 風土記 === An excerpt from the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} mentions the palace of Ōwakako no Mikoto as "Kirihara no Highetamiya" (桐原日桁宮), and attributes the origin of the name "Uji" to the establishment of this palace. However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} already records the existence of the "Uji River" (宇治川) in the annals of Emperor Suinin, this explanation is questioned,『Yamashiro Province 風土記』逸文「宇治」 (collected in 『詞林采葉抄』). and it is more likely that the name was derived from the side of Ōwakako no Mikoto.{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} === 万葉集 === The {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集}} contains the following poem, attributed to Ōwakako no Mikoto’s residence at Uji, composed as a elegy:Man'yōshū, Volume 9, Poem 1795. [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=09/1795 Man'yōshū Search System (Yamaguchi University)] {{Cquote|Elegaic Song, Uji Wakiko-no-miya Residence
Sisters, gathered on the peaks of Imaki, The spreading Tsumamatsu tree must have been seen by the ancients.
(imoragari, imaki no mine ni shigeritatsu tsumamatsu no ki wa furuhitomikemu)}} In this poem, the term "furuhito" (old person, i.e. the deceased) is interpreted to refer to Ōwakako no Mikoto.Kenji Kojima, et al., 『Man'yōshū 三』 (小学館, 1978), pp. 433-434. === その他 === Other historical texts that mention Ōwakako no Mikoto include: * The {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}}, with an entry in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【ill|815|ja|815年】) on June 27, which records the account of Gayō Hōnen, who was so moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ōwakako no Mikoto that he desired to be buried accordingly.
* An excerpt from the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 3rd year of {{ill|Tenchō|ja|天長}} (【ill|826|ja|826年】) as collected in the "Bakkuai Shokokusho" under the title "Bohai Envoy." * The {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}}, in the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}} (【ill|840|ja|840年】) on May 6, which, in discussing the scattering of the bones of Emperor Junna, refers to the tradition of scattering Ōwakako no Mikoto’s remains. * The {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} records his origins in the "Tenson Honki." * The {{ill|Engi-shiki|ja|延喜式}} in the section on {{ill|Shorinyō|ja|諸陵寮}} includes an entry on the Uji tomb (the tomb of Ōwakako no Mikoto). == 宮 == It is said that Ōwakako no Mikoto resided at the "Ujidō" (菟道宮) or "Kirihara no Highetamiya" (桐原日桁宮) as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} and the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}}. This residence is identified with either the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Jinja|ja|宇治上神社}} (located in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture) or the {{ill|Clan ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:|ja|宇治神社}} (also in Uji).According to {{Harvnb|Uji Kamigami Jinja (Heibonsha)|1981年}} and {{Harvnb|Uji (Kokushi)|1982年}}, the former is designated as the ancestral site. Together, these ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s are listed in the {{ill|Engi-shiki Shinnamyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳}} as the "two ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s of Uji, Uji-gun, Yamashiro Province." Until the Meiji period, they were regarded as one entity under the name "Uji Rikyū Myōjin." The {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集}} also contains a reference to "Uji no Miyako" (宇治乃宮子), but this is understood to refer to a temporary palace used by 【ill|Nukata no Ōkimi|ja|額田王】 during his visit to Ōmi.Man'yōshū, Volume 1, Poem 7. [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=01/0007 01/0007] (Man'yōshū Search System, Yamaguchi University) == Grave == The tomb of Ōwakako no Mikoto is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the "Uji-tomb" (宇治墓), located in the Maruyama area of Uji, Kyoto Prefecture, at the site known as the "Uji Kofun" (宇治墓) with coordinates {{ウィキ座標|34|53|50.88|N|135|48|18.49|E|region:JP-26|name=Uji Tomb (Ōwakako no Mikoto Tomb)}}.宮内省諸陵寮編 [{{NDLDC|1237123/10}} 『陵墓要覧』] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collection) 10 panels.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}}『陵墓地形図集成 縮小版』, 宮内庁書陵部陵墓課編, 学生社, 2014, p.403. The style of the tomb is that of a keyhole-shaped mound (前方後円墳) and is known as the "Maruyama Kofun." In the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, it is recorded that Ōwakako no Mikoto was interred "upon the mountain of Usagi" (菟道山上).{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} Additionally, an entry in the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} (the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}}, 840) mentions that he ordered his remains to be scattered (散骨).『続日本後紀』承和7年5月6日条 During the Edo period, the location of his tomb was unknown. In the 18th year of {{ill|Kyōhō|ja|享保}} ({{ill|1733|ja|1733年}}), based on the description in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, although no ancient tumulus was found, the summit of {{ill|Asahi-yama|ja|朝日山}} (behind the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Jinja|ja|宇治上神社}}) was identified as his burial site, and a tombstone was erected at that location.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Heibonsha)|1981年}}[http://www.kyoto-np.co.jp/info/sightseeing/mukasikatari/070119.html "Ōwakako no Mikoto Legend"] (Kyoto Newspaper, January 19, 2007) The tomb designated at the Maruyama Kofun was established in the 22nd year of {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治}} ({{ill|1889|ja|1889年}}) and has been under the administration of the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} ever since. Located on the east bank of the {{ill|Uji River|ja|宇治川}}, prior to the Meiji period it was known as "Uki-fune no Mori" (the grove of Floating Boats). Although some have argued that this differs from the "mountain top" described in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the mound was shaped into a keyhole form and designated as the Uji Tomb.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} In addition, during the designation of the tomb, a small mound nearby was identified as an ancillary burial (陪塚) for a man named {{ill|Gayō Hōnen|ja|賀陽豊年}}, who is mentioned in the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【ill|815|ja|815年】) regarding his death. According to that account, Gayō Hōnen, moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ōwakako no Mikoto, desired to be buried accordingly and was permitted by imperial decree to be interred "under the mound" (陵下).『日本後紀』弘仁6年6月27条 This identification of the ancillary mound is attributed to that decree,{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} although some interpret it as indicating Emperor Nintoku’s tomb instead.『続日本後紀 中 全現代語訳』 (講談社学術文庫, 2006) p.372 (Generally, "陵" refers to an imperial tomb, while "墓" refers to a tomb for other royal family members). Regarding the tradition of scattering his remains, while the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} records that a middle-ranking court official, {{ill|Fujiwara Yoshino|ja|藤原吉野}}, took note of it, no other historical texts mention it, leaving its veracity uncertain.Kida Sadayoshi, 「火葬と大蔵 - 焼屍・洗骨・散骨の風俗-」, 初出: 『民族と歴史 第三巻第七号』, 1919 (Taishō 8) June (via Aozora Bunko)Nakayama Tarō, 『本朝変態葬礼史』, 初出: 『犯罪科学 増刊号 異状風俗資料研究号』, 1931 (Shōwa 6) July (via Aozora Bunko) Some interpret the record as meaning that he ordered his remains to be scattered, while others suggest that his scattering set a precedent that later became customary.『続日本後紀 上 全現代語訳』 (講談社学術文庫, 2010) p.348 It is noted that in the 5th year of {{ill|Jitō Tennō|ja|持統天皇}} (【ill|691|ja|691年】), an imperial edict was issued regarding the establishment of three guard posts for the tombs of meritorious kings, suggesting that around that time, in parallel with the compilation of the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} and the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, there were moves to designate tombs based on the {{ill|Teiki|ja|帝紀}} and the {{ill|Kyūji|ja|旧辞}}. Furthermore, it is suggested that, in doing so, the tombs of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊|1=Yamato Takeru|lt=Prince Yamato Takeru|3=ヤマトタケル}} (in Ise), {{ill|Hikogase no Mikoto|ja|彦五瀬命}} (in Kii), {{ill|Itsunohoshi no Mikoto|ja|五十瓊敷入彦命}} (in Izumi), and Ōwakako no Mikoto’s tomb (in Yamashiro) were intended to form the four regional centers of Yamato.Nintō Atsushi, 「記紀から読み解く、巨大前方後円墳の編年と問題点」, 『古代史研究の最前線 天皇陵』, 洋泉社, 2016, pp.13-16. == 考証 ==

Scholars have noted that in historical texts, while there are episodes where Ōwakako no Mikoto is depicted as resorting to stratagems against his half-brother Ōyama no Mikoto, the narrative in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} especially emphasizes his self-sacrificial suicide, imbued with strong {{ill|Confucian|ja|儒教}} influences.『宇治市史 1』 (Uji City, 1973) p.210. Moreover, his mother's affiliation with the {{ill|Wae (Wa) clan|ja|和珥氏}}, the unique epithet "iratsuko," and the various expressions alluding to imperial succession highlight the singularity of his portrayal.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} Among these interpretations, some scholars argue that the descriptions of his premature death in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and his suicide in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} were later embellishments, and that he was in fact overthrown by Emperor Nintoku; this view posits that conflicts involving the Wae and {{ill|Katsuragi clan|ja|葛城氏}} underlie the narrative.Hideo Kanda's theory, as cited in {{Harvnb|Kanazawa|2007年}}. Others suggest that Ōwakako no Mikoto’s story was originally a tradition of the Wae clan, later merged with narratives of Emperor Nintoku’s consolidation of power.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}}Yuniyuki Miura, 『口語訳 古事記 完全版』 (文藝春秋, 2002) p.248, note (40). === 即位説 === In contrast to the view that portrays Ōwakako no Mikoto as a subordinate figure, some researchers propose that he may have actually ascended to the throne. Although the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} uses "iratsuko" in a manner distinct from the term for imperial heirs (as discussed above), expressions implying his reign as emperor are also found.Expressions suggesting that he was regarded as an emperor from birth, or that he was granted a reign that was later denied, such as the usage of terms like "hyakkan" and "kuzure," are noted. {{Harv|Kanazawa|2007年}} This has led to theories positing the existence of "historical facts not recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}," with Ōwakako no Mikoto potentially having reigned alongside the traditional imperial line. A similar case is seen in the figure known as "Iiohiko no Ō" (often rendered as 忍海郎女) in the context of the "Iiohiko Tennō" phenomenon, suggesting that the literary portrayal may share similar methodologies.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} Furthermore, some argue that the narrative concerning Ōwakako no Mikoto facilitates a transition from a patrilineal to a fraternal succession in the imperial lineage.Kazumi Kanazawa, [http://exam.swu.ac.jp/files/2010/05/200909-ronbun-kanazawakazumi.pdf "A Study on Uji no Wakiiratsuko and 'Ancient'"], Doctoral Dissertation Abstract, Showa Women's University, 2009. Beyond the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the {{ill|Harima-koku Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} refers to a "Uji Tennō," which some scholars believe indicates that he might have reigned as an emperor.{{Sfn|Ōwakako no Mikoto (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} == 宇治部 == As for the hereditary administrative unit (御名代部) bearing his name, the "Uji-bu" (宇治部, also read as "Ujibu") is identified as such.{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} This Uji-bu, as recorded in historical texts, is associated with the 【ill|Kabane|ja|姓】 "Ren" and is said to have been recorded in the {{ill|Shinsen Shijiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録|1=Shinsen Shōjiroku}} under the entries for the provinces of {{ill|Kawachi|ja|河内国}} and {{ill|Izumi|ja|和泉国}}. The {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} also notes that a descendant, Taben Sukune no Mikoto, was regarded as the progenitor of the Uji-bu. Although these names do not appear elsewhere,{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} some scholars argue that the descriptions in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} regarding his maternal lineage (Wae clan) might be erroneous and that his true connection lies with the Uji-bu.Ryō Ota, 『姓氏家系大辞典』 (角川書店, 1963) "Ujibu" entry, p.11. == References == === 注釈 === {{reflist|group="注"}} {{infobox noble | 氏名 = 大若子命 | 画像 = | 画像サイズ = | 画像説明 = | 時代 = |[[古墳時代]] | 生誕 = 不明 | 死没 = 不明 | 改名 = | 別名 = 大幡主命 | 諡号 = | 神号 = | 戒名 = | 墓所 = 鳥羽市沖の答志島・和具の古墳 | 官位 = 神国造、伊勢神宮初代大神主 | 主君 = |[[垂仁天皇]] | 氏族 = | 父母 = 彦久良為命[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/DAS/meta/listPhoto?LANG=default&BID=F1000000000000037305&ID=M1000000000000065387&NO=&TYPE=JPEG&DL_TYPE=pdf]『[[群書類従]]』「豊受太神宮禰宜補任次第」 | 兄弟 = 乙若子命 | 妻 = | 子 = | 特記事項 = | 花押 = }} [[ja:大若子命]] [[ja:Ōwakako no Mikoto]] '''Ōwakako no Mikoto''' (大若子命) is a legendary figure of ancient Japan appearing in texts such as {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}}. He is said to be a member of the imperial family of ancient Japan, a descendant of the first {{ill|Ise Kunizukuri|ja|伊勢国造|1=Ise no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} and en]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:d as the first chief priest of {{ill|Ise Jingū|ja|伊勢神宮}}, and is also known by the alternate name {{ill|Ohata no Mikoto|ja|大幡主命}}. == Overview == Ōwakako no Mikoto’s name does not appear in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} or the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, but is first found in texts such as the {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}}, compiled by {{ill|Dokai Gyōchū|ja|度会行忠}} of the Kamakura period.[https://kotobank.jp/word/倭姫命世記-649457 『倭姫命世紀』、コトバンク] Therefore, his deeds are considered legendary rather than historical.[https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/hyakuwa/journal.asp?record=23 「第23話 罪作りだよ？『倭姫命世紀』」 斎宮歴史博物館] According to the {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}} and the {{ill|Toyouke Ōmikūnēgi Hon'innjō|ja|豊受大神宮禰宜補任次第}}, when {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}} en]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:d Ise Jingū (the inner ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category: of Ise), he en]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:d a branch spirit ({{ill|bunrei|ja|分霊}}) from his own territory east of the {{ill|Ise Province|ja|伊勢国}} (present-day southern {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県}}, in the area known as Taketa no Kuni) to the ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:. In doing so, he assumed the title of {{ill|Kokkunzukuri|ja|神国造}} and served concurrently as the first chief priest (大神主) of Ise Jingū. Later, when he was ordered to subdue the rebellion of {{ill|Abiko|ja|阿彦}} in the former province of {{ill|Echikoku|ja|越国}} (present-day {{ill|Hokuriku|ja|北陸地方}}), he reported his success to the imperial court and was given the name "Ohata no Mikoto" (大幡主命).[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/DAS/meta/listPhoto?LANG=default&BID=F1000000000000037305&ID=M1000000000000065387&NO=&TYPE=JPEG&DL_TYPE=pdf 『群書類従』「豊受太神宮禰宜補任次第」] After the Meiji Restoration, the office of the chief priest and headship of Ise Jingū were eventually incorporated into state policy. This tradition, maintained by Ōwakako no Mikoto’s descendants, continued as part of the national religious system until reorganization during the Meiji period. == 伝説 == According to legend, although Ōwakako no Mikoto was elevated to the status of crown prince by the favor of his father, {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}}, he eventually committed suicide in order to cede the throne to his half-brother, the later {{ill|Nintoku Tennō|ja|仁徳天皇}} (also known as Ōsazaki no Mikoto). This narrative, which appears only in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, is considered a beautiful story of self-sacrifice; the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} merely records his untimely death.『古事記』及び『日本書紀』, see the relevant passages. The accounts of Ōwakako no Mikoto in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} are marked by peculiarities. For example, in the former his portrayal is highly idiosyncratic, while in the latter the narrative emphasizes his self-sacrifice. In addition, the {{ill|Harima Kokufudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} refers to him as "Uji Tennō," an appellation that has led to various interpretations. These discussions have spurred theories such as the "Emperor Accession Theory" and the "Murder by Nintoku Tennō Theory," among others.『姓氏家系大辞典』（角川書店、1963年）「宇治部」, p. 11. == 名称 == The name of Ōwakako no Mikoto is rendered differently in various documents. In this article, his name is standardized as "Ōwakako no Mikoto." * '''Uchinowakiko no Mikoto''' – as found in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} * '''Ōwakako no Mikoto Ōji''' – as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}『日本書紀』, record in the annals of {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}}. * Uji Wakiko – as an expository variant in the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} (an excerpt) * Uji Waki – as found in the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} (excerpt) * Ōwakako – as in an alternative version of the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} excerpt * Uji Wakihiko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} * Usagi no Wakiko Ōji – as recorded in the {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} "Tenson Honki" * Usagi no Wakiko – as in the {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} "Tenson Honki" * Ōwakako no Ōji – as in the {{ill|Engi-shiki|ja|延喜式}} in the section of {{ill|Shorinyō|ja|諸陵寮}} Additionally, the {{ill|Harima-koku Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} contains the name "Uji Tennō," which is also identified with Ōwakako no Mikoto. == 「ウジ」について == The element "Uji" (also read as "Uji" or "Uji" in different texts, represented by the characters 莵道/宇遅) in his name is associated with the place name {{ill|Uji|ja|宇治}} in southern {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}. The ancient form of the name "Uji" was also written as "Uji," "Udo," or "Usagi" but eventually became standardized as "Uji" during the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}}.Inoue Mitsuo, 「宇治」, 『日本古代史大辞典』 (大和書房, 2006). The {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} records that his mother, {{ill|Miyanushi Yakahaime|ja|宮主矢河枝比売}}, lived in Kobatamura (present-day {{ill|Kobata, Uji|ja|木幡}} in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture), suggesting a deep connection between Ōwakako no Mikoto and the Uji region. Even today, the place name "Usagi" remains in Uji City, though it is pronounced "Todō." In the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} excerpt, it is stated that the palace established by Ōwakako no Mikoto is the origin of the place name "Uji." However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} already mentions the "Uji River" (宇治川) in the annals of Emperor Suinin, this account is questioned,{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} and it is more likely that the name was taken from his side. Nowadays, the etymology of "Uji" is interpreted in terms of both geographical seclusion (indicated by "uchi") and political centrality in the Uji region,『宇治市史 1』 (Uji City, 1973), pp. 204-205.{{Sfn|Uji City (Heibonsha)|1981年}}. In fact, Uji is located at the northernmost periphery of the Yamato court's influence, and the legends of Ōwakako no Mikoto and the epithet "Uji Tennō" suggest the existence of a local political power in Uji.{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} There is also a theory by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}} that the name derives from "a path through a herd of rabbits"; however,Minakata Kumagusu, 「兎に関する民俗と伝説」, 『十二支考』 (岩波文庫, 1994) [Aozora Bunko version from Taishō 4, January, 『太陽』 Vol.21, No.1]. == 「イラツコ」について == The honorific "iratsuko" (郎子) attached to his name is a distinctive epithet. Although the term "iratsume" (郎女) appears frequently in historical texts (43 names in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} according to some analyses{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}}), "iratsuko" is used for only four individuals in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, including Ōwakako no Mikoto.The other three are: Ōwakako no Mikoto’s cousin, the grandson of Emperor Suinin (【ill|Itaro no Mikoto|ja|意富富杼王】); the child of Emperor Nintoku known as Hatabino Ōwakako (also called Dainichige Ō or Ōkusakami); and a child of Emperor Keitai (Ōwakako no Mikoto). This usage is peculiar and does not align with the common honorifics "mikoto" or "ō" typically attached to imperial heirs.However, in some ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s such as {{ill|Clan ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:|ja|宇治神社}}, the epithet is combined as "Ōwakako no Mikoto." There are theories suggesting that "iratsuko" functions either as an affectionate epithet or as a counterpart to "iratsume." Given that "iratsume" is often used for imperial princesses, many scholars lean toward the interpretation that "iratsuko" specifically designates an imperial prince; however, the other three individuals in question are also sometimes denoted by "ō" rather than "mikoto," suggesting that the usage leans more towards "king" than the typical "mikoto" used for heirs.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} It is also noted that the prefix "waki" (ワキ) before "iratsuko" is thought to be a corruption of "wakai" (若), meaning "young."{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} == Genealogy == === 古事記・日本書紀 === (The following names are presented with the nomenclature as first recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, with alternative names from the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and other sources noted in parentheses.) According to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ōwakako no Mikoto is the imperial son born of {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|応神天皇}} and the consort Miyanushi Yakahime (also rendered as Miyanushi Yakahaime or Miyanushi Yagahime).『古事記』, 『日本書紀』, record in the annals of Emperor Suinin. His full-siblings by the same mother include {{ill|Yata no Hime|ja|矢田皇女}} (also known as Yata no Hime or Yata Wakaro Onna) and the Hime known as Medori no Hime (女鳥王). The son of Emperor Suinin and {{ill|Nakahi no Mikoto|ja|仲姫命}} (Nakatohime no Mikoto) who later became known as {{ill|Ōsazaki no Mikoto|ja|大鷦鷯尊}} (also identified with Emperor Nintoku) is his half-brother. Also related is a figure called Onabe-hime, the sister of Miyanushi Yakahime, who gave birth to a daughter known as Ōwakako no Hime, also read as Ujinowakiko no Hime.『先代旧事本紀』, "Tenson Honki". There is no record in the historical texts regarding Ōwakako no Mikoto’s wife or children. {{皇室古墳時代}}

{{clear}} == 記録 == According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ōwakako no Mikoto learned the classics under the tutelage of 【ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐】 and 【ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁】, who were brought from {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} as tribute. However, the historical veracity of these details is uncertain.『日本書紀』 records that he learned the classics from Adochigi and Ōnin, but their historicity cannot be confirmed. [https://kotobank.jp/word/阿直岐 {{ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐}}] [https://kotobank.jp/word/王仁 {{ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁}}]. Tsuda Sayokichi regarded these as later fabrications.{{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤正二|date=2006-07-01|title=研究 on Japanese Nature: Transformation and Decline|series=斎藤正二著作選集|publisher=八坂書房|page=129}}{{Cite book|和書|author=菅原信海|date=1996-01-01|title=Japanese Thought and Syncretism|publisher=春秋社|page=24}} It is also suggested that Adochigi and Ōnin were of Chinese origin from Baekje.{{Cite book|和書|author=馬渕和夫|date=1999-01-01|title=History of the Japanese Language Studies|publisher=笠間書院|page=17}} According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, he was favored by his father, Emperor Suinin.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 15th and 16th year entries. In the 28th year of Suinin Tennō’s reign, a letter from the 【ill|Goguryeo|ja|高句麗】 pointed out an offense, which he repudiated.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 28th year, September entry. In the 40th year of Suinin Tennō’s reign (Lunisolar January), he was designated Crown Prince.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 40th year, January entry. In the following year, after the emperor's death, Ōwakako no Mikoto did not ascend the throne but instead shared the imperial succession with his half-brother, Emperor Nintoku. Amid this, his half-brother, {{ill|Ōyama no Mikoto|ja|大山守皇子}}, resentful at not being named Crown Prince, attempted to assassinate him. Ōyama no Mikoto's conspiracy was forewarned by Ōwakako no Mikoto, leading to Ōyama no Mikoto’s own demise. At that moment, a poem was composed directed at Ōyama no Mikoto’s remains:Interpretations of the classical reading and transliteration are based on the annotations and translations by Kenji Kojima, et al. in 『日本書紀』. {{Cquote|Chihayabito, across the Uji River, I shall raise the bow of catalpa wood; Though my heart wishes to strike, though it wishes to seize, In truth, I recall you, and in the far reaches, I recall my sister. In sorrow I hold you in my thoughts, yet I do not strike. (catalpa bow)} Afterward, Ōwakako no Mikoto resided at the palace known as {{ill|Ujidō no Miyako|ja|菟道宮}}, and for three years he alternated the throne with Ōyama no Mikoto. Troubled by the prospect that the long interregnum might cause national disarray, he eventually chose to end the sharing by taking his own life. In response, his half-brother was stricken with grief; from Nanba (【ill|Osaka|ja|大阪】) to Ujidō, rituals to summon the spirit were performed, and it is said that Ōwakako no Mikoto was revived, ordered that his half-sister, {{ill|Yata no Hime|ja|八田皇女}}, be received into the palace, and then passed away again.『日本書紀』, before Emperor Nintoku’s accession. === 古事記 === The {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} begins with the account of the consort, Miyanushi Yagahime (宮主矢河枝比売), who resided in Kobata (present-day {{ill|Kobata, Uji|ja|木幡}} in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture) where Emperor Suinin encountered her, leading to the birth of Ōwakako no Mikoto. Following this, the narrative aligns with that of the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. The poem composed at the time of Ōyama no Mikoto’s death is also included with almost identical wording.Annotations and transliterations are based on Kenji Kojima, et al., 『古事記』 (岩波文庫, 1963). However, regarding imperial succession, the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} simply states that Ōwakako no Mikoto died young, leading to Emperor Nintoku’s accession. === 風土記 === An excerpt from the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} mentions the palace of Ōwakako no Mikoto as "Kirihara no Highetamiya" (桐原日桁宮), and attributes the origin of the name "Uji" to the establishment of this palace. However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} already records the existence of the "Uji River" (宇治川) in the annals of Emperor Suinin, this explanation is questioned,『Yamashiro Province 風土記』逸文「宇治」 (collected in 『詞林采葉抄』). and it is more likely that the name was derived from the side of Ōwakako no Mikoto.{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} === 万葉集 === The {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集}} contains the following poem, attributed to Ōwakako no Mikoto’s residence at Uji, composed as a elegy:Man'yōshū, Volume 9, Poem 1795. [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=09/1795 Man'yōshū Search System (Yamaguchi University)] {{Cquote|Elegaic Song, Uji Wakiko-no-miya Residence
Sisters, gathered on the peaks of Imaki, The spreading Tsumamatsu tree must have been seen by the ancients.
(imoragari, imaki no mine ni shigeritatsu tsumamatsu no ki wa furuhitomikemu)}} In this poem, the term "furuhito" (old person, i.e. the deceased) is interpreted to refer to Ōwakako no Mikoto.Kenji Kojima, et al., 『Man'yōshū 三』 (小学館, 1978), pp. 433-434. === その他 === Other historical texts that mention Ōwakako no Mikoto include: * The {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}}, with an entry in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【ill|815|ja|815年】) on June 27, which records the account of Gayō Hōnen, who was so moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ōwakako no Mikoto that he desired to be buried accordingly.
* An excerpt from the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 3rd year of {{ill|Tenchō|ja|天長}} (【ill|826|ja|826年】) as collected in the "Bakkuai Shokokusho" under the title "Bohai Envoy." * The {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}}, in the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}} (【ill|840|ja|840年】) on May 6, which, in discussing the scattering of the bones of Emperor Junna, refers to the tradition of scattering Ōwakako no Mikoto’s remains. * The {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} records his origins in the "Tenson Honki." * The {{ill|Engi-shiki|ja|延喜式}} in the section on {{ill|Shorinyō|ja|諸陵寮}} includes an entry on the Uji tomb (the tomb of Ōwakako no Mikoto). == 宮 == It is said that Ōwakako no Mikoto resided at the "Ujidō" (菟道宮) or "Kirihara no Highetamiya" (桐原日桁宮) as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} and the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}}. This residence is identified with either the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Jinja|ja|宇治上神社}} (located in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture) or the {{ill|Clan ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:|ja|宇治神社}} (also in Uji).According to {{Harvnb|Uji Kamigami Jinja (Heibonsha)|1981年}} and {{Harvnb|Uji (Kokushi)|1982年}}, the former is designated as the ancestral site. Together, these ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s are listed in the {{ill|Engi-shiki Shinnamyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳}} as the "two ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s of Uji, Uji-gun, Yamashiro Province." Until the Meiji period, they were regarded as one entity under the name "Uji Rikyū Myōjin." The {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集}} also contains a reference to "Uji no Miyako" (宇治乃宮子), but this is understood to refer to a temporary palace used by 【ill|Nukata no Ōkimi|ja|額田王】 during his visit to Ōmi.Man'yōshū, Volume 1, Poem 7. [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=01/0007 01/0007] (Man'yōshū Search System, Yamaguchi University) == Grave == The tomb of Ōwakako no Mikoto is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the "Uji-tomb" (宇治墓), located in the Maruyama area of Uji, Kyoto Prefecture, at the site known as the "Uji Kofun" (宇治墓) with coordinates {{ウィキ座標|34|53|50.88|N|135|48|18.49|E|region:JP-26|name=Uji Tomb (Ōwakako no Mikoto Tomb)}}.宮内省諸陵寮編 [{{NDLDC|1237123/10}} 『陵墓要覧』] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collection) 10 panels.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}}『陵墓地形図集成 縮小版』, 宮内庁書陵部陵墓課編, 学生社, 2014, p.403. The style of the tomb is that of a keyhole-shaped mound (前方後円墳) and is known as the "Maruyama Kofun." In the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, it is recorded that Ōwakako no Mikoto was interred "upon the mountain of Usagi" (菟道山上).{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} Additionally, an entry in the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} (the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}}, 840) mentions that he ordered his remains to be scattered (散骨).『続日本後紀』承和7年5月6日条 During the Edo period, the location of his tomb was unknown. In the 18th year of {{ill|Kyōhō|ja|享保}} ({{ill|1733|ja|1733年}}), based on the description in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, although no ancient tumulus was found, the summit of {{ill|Asahi-yama|ja|朝日山}} (behind the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Jinja|ja|宇治上神社}}) was identified as his burial site, and a tombstone was erected at that location.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Heibonsha)|1981年}}[http://www.kyoto-np.co.jp/info/sightseeing/mukasikatari/070119.html "Ōwakako no Mikoto Legend"] (Kyoto Newspaper, January 19, 2007) The tomb designated at the Maruyama Kofun was established in the 22nd year of {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治}} ({{ill|1889|ja|1889年}}) and has been under the administration of the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} ever since. Located on the east bank of the {{ill|Uji River|ja|宇治川}}, prior to the Meiji period it was known as "Uki-fune no Mori" (the grove of Floating Boats). Although some have argued that this differs from the "mountain top" described in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the mound was shaped into a keyhole form and designated as the Uji Tomb.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} In addition, during the designation of the tomb, a small mound nearby was identified as an ancillary burial (陪塚) for a man named {{ill|Gayō Hōnen|ja|賀陽豊年}}, who is mentioned in the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【ill|815|ja|815年】) regarding his death. According to that account, Gayō Hōnen, moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ōwakako no Mikoto, desired to be buried accordingly and was permitted by imperial decree to be interred "under the mound" (陵下).『日本後紀』弘仁6年6月27条 This identification of the ancillary mound is attributed to that decree,{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} although some interpret it as indicating Emperor Nintoku’s tomb instead.『続日本後紀 中 全現代語訳』 (講談社学術文庫, 2006) p.372 (Generally, "陵" refers to an imperial tomb, while "墓" refers to a tomb for other royal family members). Regarding the tradition of scattering his remains, while the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} records that a middle-ranking court official, {{ill|Fujiwara Yoshino|ja|藤原吉野}}, took note of it, no other historical texts mention it, leaving its veracity uncertain.Kida Sadayoshi, 「火葬と大蔵 - 焼屍・洗骨・散骨の風俗-」, 初出: 『民族と歴史 第三巻第七号』, 1919 (Taishō 8) June (via Aozora Bunko)Nakayama Tarō, 『本朝変態葬礼史』, 初出: 『犯罪科学 増刊号 異状風俗資料研究号』, 1931 (Shōwa 6) July (via Aozora Bunko) Some interpret the record as meaning that he ordered his remains to be scattered, while others suggest that his scattering set a precedent that later became customary.『続日本後紀 上 全現代語訳』 (講談社学術文庫, 2010) p.348 It is noted that in the 5th year of {{ill|Jitō Tennō|ja|持統天皇}} (【ill|691|ja|691年】), an imperial edict was issued regarding the establishment of three guard posts for the tombs of meritorious kings, suggesting that around that time, in parallel with the compilation of the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} and the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, there were moves to designate tombs based on the {{ill|Teiki|ja|帝紀}} and the {{ill|Kyūji|ja|旧辞}}. Furthermore, it is suggested that, in doing so, the tombs of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊|1=Yamato Takeru|lt=Prince Yamato Takeru|3=ヤマトタケル}} (in Ise), {{ill|Hikogase no Mikoto|ja|彦五瀬命}} (in Kii), {{ill|Itsunohoshi no Mikoto|ja|五十瓊敷入彦命}} (in Izumi), and Ōwakako no Mikoto’s tomb (in Yamashiro) were intended to form the four regional centers of Yamato.Nintō Atsushi, 「記紀から読み解く、巨大前方後円墳の編年と問題点」, 『古代史研究の最前線 天皇陵』, 洋泉社, 2016, pp.13-16. == 考証 ==

Scholars have noted that in historical texts, while there are episodes where Ōwakako no Mikoto is depicted as resorting to stratagems against his half-brother Ōyama no Mikoto, the narrative in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} especially emphasizes his self-sacrificial suicide, imbued with strong {{ill|Confucian|ja|儒教}} influences.『宇治市史 1』 (Uji City, 1973) p.210. Moreover, his mother's affiliation with the {{ill|Wae (Wa) clan|ja|和珥氏}}, the unique epithet "iratsuko," and the various expressions alluding to imperial succession highlight the singularity of his portrayal.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} Among these interpretations, some scholars argue that the descriptions of his premature death in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and his suicide in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} were later embellishments, and that he was in fact overthrown by Emperor Nintoku; this view posits that conflicts involving the Wae and {{ill|Katsuragi clan|ja|葛城氏}} underlie the narrative.Hideo Kanda's theory, as cited in {{Harvnb|Kanazawa|2007年}}. Others suggest that Ōwakako no Mikoto’s story was originally a tradition of the Wae clan, later merged with narratives of Emperor Nintoku’s consolidation of power.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}}Yuniyuki Miura, 『口語訳 古事記 完全版』 (文藝春秋, 2002) p.248, note (40). === 即位説 === In contrast to the view that portrays Ōwakako no Mikoto as a subordinate figure, some researchers propose that he may have actually ascended to the throne. Although the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} uses "iratsuko" in a manner distinct from the term for imperial heirs (as discussed above), expressions implying his reign as emperor are also found.Expressions suggesting that he was regarded as an emperor from birth, or that he was granted a reign that was later denied, such as the usage of terms like "hyakkan" and "kuzure," are noted. {{Harv|Kanazawa|2007年}} This has led to theories positing the existence of "historical facts not recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}," with Ōwakako no Mikoto potentially having reigned alongside the traditional imperial line. A similar case is seen in the figure known as "Iiohiko no Ō" (often rendered as 忍海郎女) in the context of the "Iiohiko Tennō" phenomenon, suggesting that the literary portrayal may share similar methodologies.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} Furthermore, some argue that the narrative concerning Ōwakako no Mikoto facilitates a transition from a patrilineal to a fraternal succession in the imperial lineage.Kazumi Kanazawa, [http://exam.swu.ac.jp/files/2010/05/200909-ronbun-kanazawakazumi.pdf "A Study on Uji no Wakiiratsuko and 'Ancient'"], Doctoral Dissertation Abstract, Showa Women's University, 2009. Beyond the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the {{ill|Harima-koku Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} refers to a "Uji Tennō," which some scholars believe indicates that he might have reigned as an emperor.{{Sfn|Ōwakako no Mikoto (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} == 宇治部 == As for the hereditary administrative unit (御名代部) bearing his name, the "Uji-bu" (宇治部, also read as "Ujibu") is identified as such.{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} This Uji-bu, as recorded in historical texts, is associated with the 【ill|Kabane|ja|姓】 "Ren" and is said to have been recorded in the {{ill|Shinsen Shijiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録|1=Shinsen Shōjiroku}} under the entries for the provinces of {{ill|Kawachi|ja|河内国}} and {{ill|Izumi|ja|和泉国}}. The {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} also notes that a descendant, Taben Sukune no Mikoto, was regarded as the progenitor of the Uji-bu. Although these names do not appear elsewhere,{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} some scholars argue that the descriptions in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} regarding his maternal lineage (Wae clan) might be erroneous and that his true connection lies with the Uji-bu.Ryō Ota, 『姓氏家系大辞典』 (角川書店, 1963) "Ujibu" entry, p.11. == References == === 注釈 === {{reflist|group="注"}} {{infobox noble | 氏名 = 大若子命 | 画像 = | 画像サイズ = | 画像説明 = | 時代 = |[[古墳時代]] | 生誕 = 不明 | 死没 = 不明 | 改名 = | 別名 = 大幡主命 | 諡号 = | 神号 = | 戒名 = | 墓所 = 鳥羽市沖の答志島・和具の古墳 | 官位 = 神国造、伊勢神宮初代大神主 | 主君 = |[[垂仁天皇]] | 氏族 = | 父母 = 彦久良為命[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/DAS/meta/listPhoto?LANG=default&BID=F1000000000000037305&ID=M1000000000000065387&NO=&TYPE=JPEG&DL_TYPE=pdf]『[[群書類従]]』「豊受太神宮禰宜補任次第」 | 兄弟 = 乙若子命 | 妻 = | 子 = | 特記事項 = | 花押 = }} [[ja:大若子命]] [[ja:Ōwakako no Mikoto]] '''Ōwakako no Mikoto''' (大若子命) is a legendary figure of ancient Japan appearing in texts such as {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}}. He is said to be a member of the imperial family of ancient Japan, a descendant of the first {{ill|Ise Kunizukuri|ja|伊勢国造|1=Ise no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} and en]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:d as the first chief priest of {{ill|Ise Jingū|ja|伊勢神宮}}, and is also known by the alternate name {{ill|Ohata no Mikoto|ja|大幡主命}}. == Overview == Ōwakako no Mikoto’s name does not appear in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} or the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, but is first found in texts such as the {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}}, compiled by {{ill|Dokai Gyōchū|ja|度会行忠}} of the Kamakura period.[https://kotobank.jp/word/倭姫命世記-649457 『倭姫命世紀』、コトバンク] Therefore, his deeds are considered legendary rather than historical.[https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/hyakuwa/journal.asp?record=23 「第23話 罪作りだよ？『倭姫命世紀』」 斎宮歴史博物館] According to the {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}} and the {{ill|Toyouke Ōmikūnēgi Hon'innjō|ja|豊受大神宮禰宜補任次第}}, when {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}} en]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:d Ise Jingū (the inner ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category: of Ise), he en]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:d a branch spirit ({{ill|bunrei|ja|分霊}}) from his own territory east of the {{ill|Ise Province|ja|伊勢国}} (present-day southern {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県}}, in the area known as Taketa no Kuni) to the ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:. In doing so, he assumed the title of {{ill|Kokkunzukuri|ja|神国造}} and served concurrently as the first chief priest (大神主) of Ise Jingū. Later, when he was ordered to subdue the rebellion of {{ill|Abiko|ja|阿彦}} in the former province of {{ill|Echikoku|ja|越国}} (present-day {{ill|Hokuriku|ja|北陸地方}}), he reported his success to the imperial court and was given the name "Ohata no Mikoto" (大幡主命).[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/DAS/meta/listPhoto?LANG=default&BID=F1000000000000037305&ID=M1000000000000065387&NO=&TYPE=JPEG&DL_TYPE=pdf 『群書類従』「豊受太神宮禰宜補任次第」] After the Meiji Restoration, the office of the chief priest and headship of Ise Jingū were eventually incorporated into state policy. This tradition, maintained by Ōwakako no Mikoto’s descendants, continued as part of the national religious system until reorganization during the Meiji period. == 伝説 == According to legend, although Ōwakako no Mikoto was elevated to the status of crown prince by the favor of his father, {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}}, he eventually committed suicide in order to cede the throne to his half-brother, the later {{ill|Nintoku Tennō|ja|仁徳天皇}} (also known as Ōsazaki no Mikoto). This narrative, which appears only in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, is considered a beautiful story of self-sacrifice; the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} merely records his untimely death.『古事記』及び『日本書紀』, see the relevant passages. The accounts of Ōwakako no Mikoto in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} are marked by peculiarities. For example, in the former his portrayal is highly idiosyncratic, while in the latter the narrative emphasizes his self-sacrifice. In addition, the {{ill|Harima Kokufudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} refers to him as "Uji Tennō," an appellation that has led to various interpretations. These discussions have spurred theories such as the "Emperor Accession Theory" and the "Murder by Nintoku Tennō Theory," among others.『姓氏家系大辞典』（角川書店、1963年）「宇治部」, p. 11. == 名称 == The name of Ōwakako no Mikoto is rendered differently in various documents. In this article, his name is standardized as "Ōwakako no Mikoto." * '''Uchinowakiko no Mikoto''' – as found in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} * '''Ōwakako no Mikoto Ōji''' – as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}『日本書紀』, record in the annals of {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}}. * Uji Wakiko – as an expository variant in the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} (an excerpt) * Uji Waki – as found in the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} (excerpt) * Ōwakako – as in an alternative version of the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} excerpt * Uji Wakihiko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} * Usagi no Wakiko Ōji – as recorded in the {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} "Tenson Honki" * Usagi no Wakiko – as in the {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} "Tenson Honki" * Ōwakako no Ōji – as in the {{ill|Engi-shiki|ja|延喜式}} in the section of {{ill|Shorinyō|ja|諸陵寮}} Additionally, the {{ill|Harima-koku Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} contains the name "Uji Tennō," which is also identified with Ōwakako no Mikoto. == 「ウジ」について == The element "Uji" (also read as "Uji" or "Uji" in different texts, represented by the characters 莵道/宇遅) in his name is associated with the place name {{ill|Uji|ja|宇治}} in southern {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}. The ancient form of the name "Uji" was also written as "Uji," "Udo," or "Usagi" but eventually became standardized as "Uji" during the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}}.Inoue Mitsuo, 「宇治」, 『日本古代史大辞典』 (大和書房, 2006). The {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} records that his mother, {{ill|Miyanushi Yakahaime|ja|宮主矢河枝比売}}, lived in Kobatamura (present-day {{ill|Kobata, Uji|ja|木幡}} in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture), suggesting a deep connection between Ōwakako no Mikoto and the Uji region. Even today, the place name "Usagi" remains in Uji City, though it is pronounced "Todō." In the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} excerpt, it is stated that the palace established by Ōwakako no Mikoto is the origin of the place name "Uji." However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} already mentions the "Uji River" (宇治川) in the annals of Emperor Suinin, this account is questioned,{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} and it is more likely that the name was taken from his side. Nowadays, the etymology of "Uji" is interpreted in terms of both geographical seclusion (indicated by "uchi") and political centrality in the Uji region,『宇治市史 1』 (Uji City, 1973), pp. 204-205.{{Sfn|Uji City (Heibonsha)|1981年}}. In fact, Uji is located at the northernmost periphery of the Yamato court's influence, and the legends of Ōwakako no Mikoto and the epithet "Uji Tennō" suggest the existence of a local political power in Uji.{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} There is also a theory by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}} that the name derives from "a path through a herd of rabbits"; however,Minakata Kumagusu, 「兎に関する民俗と伝説」, 『十二支考』 (岩波文庫, 1994) [Aozora Bunko version from Taishō 4, January, 『太陽』 Vol.21, No.1]. == 「イラツコ」について == The honorific "iratsuko" (郎子) attached to his name is a distinctive epithet. Although the term "iratsume" (郎女) appears frequently in historical texts (43 names in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} according to some analyses{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}}), "iratsuko" is used for only four individuals in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, including Ōwakako no Mikoto.The other three are: Ōwakako no Mikoto’s cousin, the grandson of Emperor Suinin (【ill|Itaro no Mikoto|ja|意富富杼王】); the child of Emperor Nintoku known as Hatabino Ōwakako (also called Dainichige Ō or Ōkusakami); and a child of Emperor Keitai (Ōwakako no Mikoto). This usage is peculiar and does not align with the common honorifics "mikoto" or "ō" typically attached to imperial heirs.However, in some ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s such as {{ill|Clan ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:|ja|宇治神社}}, the epithet is combined as "Ōwakako no Mikoto." There are theories suggesting that "iratsuko" functions either as an affectionate epithet or as a counterpart to "iratsume." Given that "iratsume" is often used for imperial princesses, many scholars lean toward the interpretation that "iratsuko" specifically designates an imperial prince; however, the other three individuals in question are also sometimes denoted by "ō" rather than "mikoto," suggesting that the usage leans more towards "king" than the typical "mikoto" used for heirs.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} It is also noted that the prefix "waki" (ワキ) before "iratsuko" is thought to be a corruption of "wakai" (若), meaning "young."{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} == Genealogy == === 古事記・日本書紀 === (The following names are presented with the nomenclature as first recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, with alternative names from the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and other sources noted in parentheses.) According to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ōwakako no Mikoto is the imperial son born of {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|応神天皇}} and the consort Miyanushi Yakahime (also rendered as Miyanushi Yakahaime or Miyanushi Yagahime).『古事記』, 『日本書紀』, record in the annals of Emperor Suinin. His full-siblings by the same mother include {{ill|Yata no Hime|ja|矢田皇女}} (also known as Yata no Hime or Yata Wakaro Onna) and the Hime known as Medori no Hime (女鳥王). The son of Emperor Suinin and {{ill|Nakahi no Mikoto|ja|仲姫命}} (Nakatohime no Mikoto) who later became known as {{ill|Ōsazaki no Mikoto|ja|大鷦鷯尊}} (also identified with Emperor Nintoku) is his half-brother. Also related is a figure called Onabe-hime, the sister of Miyanushi Yakahime, who gave birth to a daughter known as Ōwakako no Hime, also read as Ujinowakiko no Hime.『先代旧事本紀』, "Tenson Honki". There is no record in the historical texts regarding Ōwakako no Mikoto’s wife or children. {{皇室古墳時代}}

{{clear}} == 記録 == According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ōwakako no Mikoto learned the classics under the tutelage of 【ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐】 and 【ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁】, who were brought from {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} as tribute. However, the historical veracity of these details is uncertain.『日本書紀』 records that he learned the classics from Adochigi and Ōnin, but their historicity cannot be confirmed. [https://kotobank.jp/word/阿直岐 {{ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐}}] [https://kotobank.jp/word/王仁 {{ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁}}]. Tsuda Sayokichi regarded these as later fabrications.{{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤正二|date=2006-07-01|title=研究 on Japanese Nature: Transformation and Decline|series=斎藤正二著作選集|publisher=八坂書房|page=129}}{{Cite book|和書|author=菅原信海|date=1996-01-01|title=Japanese Thought and Syncretism|publisher=春秋社|page=24}} It is also suggested that Adochigi and Ōnin were of Chinese origin from Baekje.{{Cite book|和書|author=馬渕和夫|date=1999-01-01|title=History of the Japanese Language Studies|publisher=笠間書院|page=17}} According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, he was favored by his father, Emperor Suinin.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 15th and 16th year entries. In the 28th year of Suinin Tennō’s reign, a letter from the 【ill|Goguryeo|ja|高句麗】 pointed out an offense, which he repudiated.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 28th year, September entry. In the 40th year of Suinin Tennō’s reign (Lunisolar January), he was designated Crown Prince.『日本書紀』, Suinin Tennō 40th year, January entry. In the following year, after the emperor's death, Ōwakako no Mikoto did not ascend the throne but instead shared the imperial succession with his half-brother, Emperor Nintoku. Amid this, his half-brother, {{ill|Ōyama no Mikoto|ja|大山守皇子}}, resentful at not being named Crown Prince, attempted to assassinate him. Ōyama no Mikoto's conspiracy was forewarned by Ōwakako no Mikoto, leading to Ōyama no Mikoto’s own demise. At that moment, a poem was composed directed at Ōyama no Mikoto’s remains:Interpretations of the classical reading and transliteration are based on the annotations and translations by Kenji Kojima, et al. in 『日本書紀』. {{Cquote|Chihayabito, across the Uji River, I shall raise the bow of catalpa wood; Though my heart wishes to strike, though it wishes to seize, In truth, I recall you, and in the far reaches, I recall my sister. In sorrow I hold you in my thoughts, yet I do not strike. (catalpa bow)} Afterward, Ōwakako no Mikoto resided at the palace known as {{ill|Ujidō no Miyako|ja|菟道宮}}, and for three years he alternated the throne with Ōyama no Mikoto. Troubled by the prospect that the long interregnum might cause national disarray, he eventually chose to end the sharing by taking his own life. In response, his half-brother was stricken with grief; from Nanba (【ill|Osaka|ja|大阪】) to Ujidō, rituals to summon the spirit were performed, and it is said that Ōwakako no Mikoto was revived, ordered that his half-sister, {{ill|Yata no Hime|ja|八田皇女}}, be received into the palace, and then passed away again.『日本書紀』, before Emperor Nintoku’s accession. === 古事記 === The {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} begins with the account of the consort, Miyanushi Yagahime (宮主矢河枝比売), who resided in Kobata (present-day {{ill|Kobata, Uji|ja|木幡}} in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture) where Emperor Suinin encountered her, leading to the birth of Ōwakako no Mikoto. Following this, the narrative aligns with that of the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. The poem composed at the time of Ōyama no Mikoto’s death is also included with almost identical wording.Annotations and transliterations are based on Kenji Kojima, et al., 『古事記』 (岩波文庫, 1963). However, regarding imperial succession, the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} simply states that Ōwakako no Mikoto died young, leading to Emperor Nintoku’s accession. === 風土記 === An excerpt from the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} mentions the palace of Ōwakako no Mikoto as "Kirihara no Highetamiya" (桐原日桁宮), and attributes the origin of the name "Uji" to the establishment of this palace. However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} already records the existence of the "Uji River" (宇治川) in the annals of Emperor Suinin, this explanation is questioned,『Yamashiro Province 風土記』逸文「宇治」 (collected in 『詞林采葉抄』). and it is more likely that the name was derived from the side of Ōwakako no Mikoto.{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} === 万葉集 === The {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集}} contains the following poem, attributed to Ōwakako no Mikoto’s residence at Uji, composed as a elegy:Man'yōshū, Volume 9, Poem 1795. [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=09/1795 Man'yōshū Search System (Yamaguchi University)] {{Cquote|Elegaic Song, Uji Wakiko-no-miya Residence
Sisters, gathered on the peaks of Imaki, The spreading Tsumamatsu tree must have been seen by the ancients.
(imoragari, imaki no mine ni shigeritatsu tsumamatsu no ki wa furuhitomikemu)}} In this poem, the term "furuhito" (old person, i.e. the deceased) is interpreted to refer to Ōwakako no Mikoto.Kenji Kojima, et al., 『Man'yōshū 三』 (小学館, 1978), pp. 433-434. === その他 === Other historical texts that mention Ōwakako no Mikoto include: * The {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}}, with an entry in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【ill|815|ja|815年】) on June 27, which records the account of Gayō Hōnen, who was so moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ōwakako no Mikoto that he desired to be buried accordingly.
* An excerpt from the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 3rd year of {{ill|Tenchō|ja|天長}} (【ill|826|ja|826年】) as collected in the "Bakkuai Shokokusho" under the title "Bohai Envoy." * The {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}}, in the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}} (【ill|840|ja|840年】) on May 6, which, in discussing the scattering of the bones of Emperor Junna, refers to the tradition of scattering Ōwakako no Mikoto’s remains. * The {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} records his origins in the "Tenson Honki." * The {{ill|Engi-shiki|ja|延喜式}} in the section on {{ill|Shorinyō|ja|諸陵寮}} includes an entry on the Uji tomb (the tomb of Ōwakako no Mikoto). == 宮 == It is said that Ōwakako no Mikoto resided at the "Ujidō" (菟道宮) or "Kirihara no Highetamiya" (桐原日桁宮) as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} and the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}}. This residence is identified with either the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Jinja|ja|宇治上神社}} (located in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture) or the {{ill|Clan ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:|ja|宇治神社}} (also in Uji).According to {{Harvnb|Uji Kamigami Jinja (Heibonsha)|1981年}} and {{Harvnb|Uji (Kokushi)|1982年}}, the former is designated as the ancestral site. Together, these ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s are listed in the {{ill|Engi-shiki Shinnamyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳}} as the "two ]][[Category:shrine pages to be written]][[Category:s of Uji, Uji-gun, Yamashiro Province." Until the Meiji period, they were regarded as one entity under the name "Uji Rikyū Myōjin." The {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集}} also contains a reference to "Uji no Miyako" (宇治乃宮子), but this is understood to refer to a temporary palace used by 【ill|Nukata no Ōkimi|ja|額田王】 during his visit to Ōmi.Man'yōshū, Volume 1, Poem 7. [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=01/0007 01/0007] (Man'yōshū Search System, Yamaguchi University) == Grave == The tomb of Ōwakako no Mikoto is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the "Uji-tomb" (宇治墓), located in the Maruyama area of Uji, Kyoto Prefecture, at the site known as the "Uji Kofun" (宇治墓) with coordinates {{ウィキ座標|34|53|50.88|N|135|48|18.49|E|region:JP-26|name=Uji Tomb (Ōwakako no Mikoto Tomb)}}.宮内省諸陵寮編 [{{NDLDC|1237123/10}} 『陵墓要覧』] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collection) 10 panels.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}}『陵墓地形図集成 縮小版』, 宮内庁書陵部陵墓課編, 学生社, 2014, p.403. The style of the tomb is that of a keyhole-shaped mound (前方後円墳) and is known as the "Maruyama Kofun." In the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, it is recorded that Ōwakako no Mikoto was interred "upon the mountain of Usagi" (菟道山上).{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} Additionally, an entry in the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} (the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}}, 840) mentions that he ordered his remains to be scattered (散骨).『続日本後紀』承和7年5月6日条 During the Edo period, the location of his tomb was unknown. In the 18th year of {{ill|Kyōhō|ja|享保}} ({{ill|1733|ja|1733年}}), based on the description in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, although no ancient tumulus was found, the summit of {{ill|Asahi-yama|ja|朝日山}} (behind the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Jinja|ja|宇治上神社}}) was identified as his burial site, and a tombstone was erected at that location.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Heibonsha)|1981年}}[http://www.kyoto-np.co.jp/info/sightseeing/mukasikatari/070119.html "Ōwakako no Mikoto Legend"] (Kyoto Newspaper, January 19, 2007) The tomb designated at the Maruyama Kofun was established in the 22nd year of {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治}} ({{ill|1889|ja|1889年}}) and has been under the administration of the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} ever since. Located on the east bank of the {{ill|Uji River|ja|宇治川}}, prior to the Meiji period it was known as "Uki-fune no Mori" (the grove of Floating Boats). Although some have argued that this differs from the "mountain top" described in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the mound was shaped into a keyhole form and designated as the Uji Tomb.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} In addition, during the designation of the tomb, a small mound nearby was identified as an ancillary burial (陪塚) for a man named {{ill|Gayō Hōnen|ja|賀陽豊年}}, who is mentioned in the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【ill|815|ja|815年】) regarding his death. According to that account, Gayō Hōnen, moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ōwakako no Mikoto, desired to be buried accordingly and was permitted by imperial decree to be interred "under the mound" (陵下).『日本後紀』弘仁6年6月27条 This identification of the ancillary mound is attributed to that decree,{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982年}} although some interpret it as indicating Emperor Nintoku’s tomb instead.『続日本後紀 中 全現代語訳』 (講談社学術文庫, 2006) p.372 (Generally, "陵" refers to an imperial tomb, while "墓" refers to a tomb for other royal family members). Regarding the tradition of scattering his remains, while the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} records that a middle-ranking court official, {{ill|Fujiwara Yoshino|ja|藤原吉野}}, took note of it, no other historical texts mention it, leaving its veracity uncertain.Kida Sadayoshi, 「火葬と大蔵 - 焼屍・洗骨・散骨の風俗-」, 初出: 『民族と歴史 第三巻第七号』, 1919 (Taishō 8) June (via Aozora Bunko)Nakayama Tarō, 『本朝変態葬礼史』, 初出: 『犯罪科学 増刊号 異状風俗資料研究号』, 1931 (Shōwa 6) July (via Aozora Bunko) Some interpret the record as meaning that he ordered his remains to be scattered, while others suggest that his scattering set a precedent that later became customary.『続日本後紀 上 全現代語訳』 (講談社学術文庫, 2010) p.348 It is noted that in the 5th year of {{ill|Jitō Tennō|ja|持統天皇}} (【ill|691|ja|691年】), an imperial edict was issued regarding the establishment of three guard posts for the tombs of meritorious kings, suggesting that around that time, in parallel with the compilation of the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} and the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, there were moves to designate tombs based on the {{ill|Teiki|ja|帝紀}} and the {{ill|Kyūji|ja|旧辞}}. Furthermore, it is suggested that, in doing so, the tombs of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊|1=Yamato Takeru|lt=Prince Yamato Takeru|3=ヤマトタケル}} (in Ise), {{ill|Hikogase no Mikoto|ja|彦五瀬命}} (in Kii), {{ill|Itsunohoshi no Mikoto|ja|五十瓊敷入彦命}} (in Izumi), and Ōwakako no Mikoto’s tomb (in Yamashiro) were intended to form the four regional centers of Yamato.Nintō Atsushi, 「記紀から読み解く、巨大前方後円墳の編年と問題点」, 『古代史研究の最前線 天皇陵』, 洋泉社, 2016, pp.13-16. == 考証 ==

Scholars have noted that in historical texts, while there are episodes where Ōwakako no Mikoto is depicted as resorting to stratagems against his half-brother Ōyama no Mikoto, the narrative in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} especially emphasizes his self-sacrificial suicide, imbued with strong {{ill|Confucian|ja|儒教}} influences.『宇治市史 1』 (Uji City, 1973) p.210. Moreover, his mother's affiliation with the {{ill|Wae (Wa) clan|ja|和珥氏}}, the unique epithet "iratsuko," and the various expressions alluding to imperial succession highlight the singularity of his portrayal.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} Among these interpretations, some scholars argue that the descriptions of his premature death in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and his suicide in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} were later embellishments, and that he was in fact overthrown by Emperor Nintoku; this view posits that conflicts involving the Wae and {{ill|Katsuragi clan|ja|葛城氏}} underlie the narrative.Hideo Kanda's theory, as cited in {{Harvnb|Kanazawa|2007年}}. Others suggest that Ōwakako no Mikoto’s story was originally a tradition of the Wae clan, later merged with narratives of Emperor Nintoku’s consolidation of power.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}}Yuniyuki Miura, 『口語訳 古事記 完全版』 (文藝春秋, 2002) p.248, note (40). === 即位説 === In contrast to the view that portrays Ōwakako no Mikoto as a subordinate figure, some researchers propose that he may have actually ascended to the throne. Although the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} uses "iratsuko" in a manner distinct from the term for imperial heirs (as discussed above), expressions implying his reign as emperor are also found.Expressions suggesting that he was regarded as an emperor from birth, or that he was granted a reign that was later denied, such as the usage of terms like "hyakkan" and "kuzure," are noted. {{Harv|Kanazawa|2007年}} This has led to theories positing the existence of "historical facts not recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}," with Ōwakako no Mikoto potentially having reigned alongside the traditional imperial line. A similar case is seen in the figure known as "Iiohiko no Ō" (often rendered as 忍海郎女) in the context of the "Iiohiko Tennō" phenomenon, suggesting that the literary portrayal may share similar methodologies.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} Furthermore, some argue that the narrative concerning Ōwakako no Mikoto facilitates a transition from a patrilineal to a fraternal succession in the imperial lineage.Kazumi Kanazawa, [http://exam.swu.ac.jp/files/2010/05/200909-ronbun-kanazawakazumi.pdf "A Study on Uji no Wakiiratsuko and 'Ancient'"], Doctoral Dissertation Abstract, Showa Women's University, 2009. Beyond the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the {{ill|Harima-koku Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} refers to a "Uji Tennō," which some scholars believe indicates that he might have reigned as an emperor.{{Sfn|Ōwakako no Mikoto (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} == 宇治部 == As for the hereditary administrative unit (御名代部) bearing his name, the "Uji-bu" (宇治部, also read as "Ujibu") is identified as such.{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} This Uji-bu, as recorded in historical texts, is associated with the 【ill|Kabane|ja|姓】 "Ren" and is said to have been recorded in the {{ill|Shinsen Shijiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録|1=Shinsen Shōjiroku}} under the entries for the provinces of {{ill|Kawachi|ja|河内国}} and {{ill|Izumi|ja|和泉国}}. The {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} also notes that a descendant, Taben Sukune no Mikoto, was regarded as the progenitor of the Uji-bu. Although these names do not appear elsewhere,{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010年}} some scholars argue that the descriptions in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} regarding his maternal lineage (Wae clan) might be erroneous and that his true connection lies with the Uji-bu.Ryō Ota, 『姓氏家系大辞典』 (角川書店, 1963) "Ujibu" entry, p.11. == References == === 注釈 === {{reflist|group="注"}} {{infobox noble | 氏名 = 大若子命 | 画像 = | 画像サイズ = | 画像説明 = | 時代 = |[[古墳時代]] | 生誕 = 不明 | 死没 = 不明 | 改名 = | 別名 = 大幡主命 | 諡号 = | 神号 = | 戒名 = | 墓所 = 鳥羽市沖の答志島・和具の古墳 | 官位 = 神国造、伊勢神宮初代大神主 | 主君 = |[[垂仁天皇]] | 氏族 = | 父母 = 彦久良為命[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/DAS/meta/listPhoto?LANG=default&BID=F1000000000000037305&ID=M1000000000000065387&NO=&TYPE=JPEG&DL_TYPE=pdf]『[[群書類従]]』「豊受太神宮禰宜補任次第」 | 兄弟 = 乙若子命 | 妻 = | 子 = | 特記事項 = | 花押 = }} [[ja:大若子命]] [[ja:Ōwakako no Mikoto]] '''Ōwakako no Mikoto''' (大若子命) is a legendary figure of ancient Japan appearing in texts such as {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}}. He is said to be a member of the imperial family of ancient Japan, a descendant of the first {{ill|Ise Kunizukuri|ja|伊勢国造|1=Ise no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} and en]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:d as the first chief priest of {{ill|Ise Jingū|ja|伊勢神宮}}, and is also known by the alternate name {{ill|Ohata no Mikoto|ja|大幡主命}}. == Overview == Ōwakako no Mikoto’s name does not appear in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} or the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, but is first found in texts such as the {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}}, compiled by {{ill|Dokai Gyōchū|ja|度会行忠}} of the Kamakura period.[https://kotobank.jp/word/倭姫命世記-649457 『倭姫命世紀』、コトバンク] Therefore, his deeds are considered legendary rather than historical.[https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/hyakuwa/journal.asp?record=23 「第23話 罪作りだよ？『倭姫命世紀』」 斎宮歴史博物館] According to the {{ill|Wakihime-myo-seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki}} and the {{ill|Toyouke Ōmikūnēgi Hon'innjō|ja|豊受大神宮禰宜補任次第}}, when {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}} en]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:. In doing so, he assumed the title of {{ill|Kokkunzukuri|ja|神国造}} and served concurrently as the first chief priest (大神主) of Ise Jingū. Later, when he was ordered to subdue the rebellion of {{ill|Abiko|ja|阿彦}} in the former province of {{ill|Echikoku|ja|越国}} (present-day {{ill|Hokuriku|ja|北陸地方}}), he reported his success to the imperial court and was given the name "Ohata no Mikoto" (大幡主命).[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/DAS/meta/listPhoto?LANG=default&BID=F1000000000000037305&ID=M1000000000000065387&NO=&TYPE=JPEG&DL_TYPE=pdf 『群書類従』「豊受太神宮禰宜補任次第」] After the Meiji Restoration, the office of the chief priest and headship of Ise Jingū were eventually incorporated into state policy. This tradition, maintained by Ōwakako no Mikoto’s descendants, continued as part of the national religious system until reorganization during the Meiji period. == 伝説 == According to legend, although Ōwakako no Mikoto was elevated to the status of crown prince by the favor of his father, {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}}, he eventually committed suicide in order to cede the throne to his half-brother, the later {{ill|Nintoku Tennō|ja|仁徳天皇}} (also known as Ōsazaki no Mikoto). This narrative, which appears only in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, is considered a beautiful story of self-sacrifice; the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} merely records his untimely death.『古事記』及び『日本書紀』, see the relevant passages. The accounts of Ōwakako no Mikoto in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} are marked by peculiarities. For example, in the former his portrayal is highly idiosyncratic, while in the latter the narrative emphasizes his self-sacrifice. In addition, the {{ill|Harima Kokufudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} refers to him as "Uji Tennō," an appellation that has led to various interpretations. These discussions have spurred theories such as the "Emperor Accession Theory" and the "Murder by Nintoku Tennō Theory," among others.『姓氏家系大辞典』（角川書店、1963年）「宇治部」, p. 11. == 名称 == The name of Ōwakako no Mikoto is rendered differently in various documents. In this article, his name is standardized as "Ōwakako no Mikoto." * '''Uchinowakiko no Mikoto''' – as found in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} * '''Ōwakako no Mikoto Ōji''' – as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}『日本書紀』, record in the annals of {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|垂仁天皇}}. * Uji Wakiko – as an expository variant in the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} (an excerpt) * Uji Waki – as found in the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} (excerpt) * Ōwakako – as in an alternative version of the {{ill|Nihongo Kōki|ja|日本後紀}} excerpt * Uji Wakihiko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Zoku Nihongo Kōki|ja|続日本後紀}} * Usagi no Wakiko Ōji – as recorded in the {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} "Tenson Honki" * Usagi no Wakiko – as in the {{ill|Sendai Kyūjihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} "Tenson Honki" * Ōwakako no Ōji – as in the {{ill|Engi-shiki|ja|延喜式}} in the section of {{ill|Shorinyō|ja|諸陵寮}} Additionally, the {{ill|Harima-koku Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} contains the name "Uji Tennō," which is also identified with Ōwakako no Mikoto. == 「ウジ」について == The element "Uji" (also read as "Uji" or "Uji" in different texts, represented by the characters 莵道/宇遅) in his name is associated with the place name {{ill|Uji|ja|宇治}} in southern {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}. The ancient form of the name "Uji" was also written as "Uji," "Udo," or "Usagi" but eventually became standardized as "Uji" during the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}}.Inoue Mitsuo, 「宇治」, 『日本古代史大辞典』 (大和書房, 2006). The {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} records that his mother, {{ill|Miyanushi Yakahaime|ja|宮主矢河枝比売}}, lived in Kobatamura (present-day {{ill|Kobata, Uji|ja|木幡}} in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, Kyoto Prefecture), suggesting a deep connection between Ōwakako no Mikoto and the Uji region. Even today, the place name "Usagi" remains in Uji City, though it is pronounced "Todō." In the {{ill|Yamashiro-koku Fudoki|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} excerpt, it is stated that the palace established by Ōwakako no Mikoto is the origin of the place name "Uji." However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} already mentions the "Uji River" (宇治川) in the annals of Emperor Suinin, this account is questioned,{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} and it is more likely that the name was taken from his side. Nowadays, the etymology of "Uji" is interpreted in terms of both geographical seclusion (indicated by "uchi") and political centrality in the Uji region,『宇治市史 1』 (Uji City, 1973), pp. 204-205.{{Sfn|Uji City (Heibonsha)|1981年}}. In fact, Uji is located at the northernmost periphery of the Yamato court's influence, and the legends of Ōwakako no Mikoto and the epithet "Uji Tennō" suggest the existence of a local political power in Uji.{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982年}} There is also a theory by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}} that the name derives from "a path through a herd of rabbits"; however,Minakata Kumagusu, 「兎に関する民俗と伝説」, 『十二支考』 (岩波文庫, 1994) [Aozora Bunko version from Taishō 4, January, 『太陽』 Vol.21, No.1]. == 「イラツコ」について == The honorific "iratsuko" (郎子) attached to his name is a distinctive epithet. Although the term "iratsume" (郎女) appears frequently in historical texts (43 names in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} according to some analyses{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}}), "iratsuko" is used for only four individuals in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, including Ōwakako no Mikoto.The other three are: Ōwakako no Mikoto’s cousin, the grandson of Emperor Suinin (【ill|Itaro no Mikoto|ja|意富富杼王】); the child of Emperor Nintoku known as Hatabino Ōwakako (also called Dainichige Ō or Ōkusakami); and a child of Emperor Keitai (Ōwakako no Mikoto). This usage is peculiar and does not align with the common honorifics "mikoto" or "ō" typically attached to imperial heirs.However, in some ]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:Shrine pages to be written]][[Category:|ja|宇治神社}}, the epithet is combined as "Ōwakako no Mikoto." There are theories suggesting that "iratsuko" functions either as an affectionate epithet or as a counterpart to "iratsume." Given that "iratsume" is often used for imperial princesses, many scholars lean toward the interpretation that "iratsuko" specifically designates an imperial prince; however, the other three individuals in question are also sometimes denoted by "ō" rather than "mikoto," suggesting that the usage leans more towards "king" than the typical "mikoto" used for heirs.{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} It is also noted that the prefix "waki" (ワキ) before "iratsuko" is thought to be a corruption of "wakai" (若), meaning "young."{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007年}} == Genealogy == === 古事記・日本書紀 === (The following names are presented with the nomenclature as first recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, with alternative names from the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and other sources noted in parentheses.) According to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ōwakako no Mikoto is the imperial son born of {{ill|Suinin Tennō|ja|応神天皇}} and the consort Miyanushi Yakahime (also rendered as Miyanushi Yakahaime or Miyanushi Yagahime).『古事記』, 『日本書紀』, record in the annals of Emperor Suinin. His full-siblings by the same mother include {{ill|Yata no Hime|ja|矢田皇女}} (also known as Yata no Hime or Yata Wakaro Onna) and the Hime known as Medori no Hime (女鳥王). The son of Emperor Suinin and {{ill|Nakahi no Mikoto|ja|仲姫命}} (Nakatohime no Mikoto) who later became known as {{ill|Ōsazaki no Mikoto|ja|大鷦鷯尊}} (also identified with Emperor Nintoku) is his half-brother. Also related is a figure called Onabe-hime, the sister of Miyanushi Yakahime, who gave birth to a daughter known as Ōwakako no Hime, also read as Ujinowakiko no Hime.『先代旧事本紀』, "Tenson Honki". There is no record in the historical texts regarding Ōwakako no Mikoto’s wife or children. {{皇室古墳時代}}
